comunicacion.metaDescription: Communication axis — media literacy: media ecosystem, freedom of expression, mass media, disinformation (information integrity), and social networks.

It’s not just about traditional media, but about the entire ecosystem that produces, distributes, and reshapes the information we consume daily—from a news bulletin to a meme on social networks.

This axis proposes looking closely at the path information travels, questioning who produces it, why, and with what intention. It also invites us to strengthen the right to express ourselves, to inform ourselves freely, and to recognise when that right is at risk—through censorship, disinformation (information integrity), or the invisibilisation of certain communities.

cultura.metaDescription: Culture axis — media literacy: cultural diversity, media representation, digital culture, participation, dialogue, and the right to communicate.
cultura.heroIntro: Culture is identity, memory, and creation. Media literacy lets us inhabit that space with awareness and a voice of our own.
paras: Culture is not an ornament: it’s the way we live together, recognise each other, and express ourselves. It’s in what we consume, how we speak, in the memes we share, in the stories we inherit and in those we decide to transform.

In the digital environment, culture multiplies and changes rapidly. Youth narratives, viral content, expressions from native peoples, women’s activism, digital aesthetics, and public debates on networks are as much part of the cultural field as a book, a festival, or a work of art.

Media literacy enters here not to judge but to expand. It gives us tools to understand which meanings are reproduced, which are made invisible, and how we can intervene in creative, respectful, and transformative ways.

A cultural approach to media literacy recognises the right to communicate from diversity, fosters intergenerational dialogue, and promotes a citizenry able to build its own narratives, beyond hegemonic discourses.

educacion.metaDescription: Education axis — media literacy: critical thinking, classroom, production, information assessment, and digital life.
educacion.heroIntro: This axis seeks to transform the relationship between citizenry and media from the root: critical thinking, lifelong learning, and the capacity to act with awareness in the public sphere.
educacion.subhead: Learning throughout life to live in a critical, conscious, and active digital environment
paras: This axis focuses on building media competencies from childhood through older adulthood. It’s not just about teaching how to use technology, but about shaping a citizenry able to understand, analyse, and take part in building the digital and informational world.

Media literacy, in this sense, is a tool for autonomy and participation that should be present throughout life: in childhood, as a basis for critical reading; in adolescence, to strengthen digital identity; in adulthood, to defend against disinformation (information integrity) and make informed decisions; and in old age, to ensure inclusion, bonds, and rights.
listItems: Integrating media and information literacy into school curricula, not as an isolated subject but as a cross-cutting competence.
Supporting teachers and educators with contextualised tools, methodologies, and content.
Creative and reflective content production (videos, podcasts, memes, articles) as a way of learning by doing.
Developing critical thinking, informational reading, and skills to navigate digital environments.
Promoting training spaces for adults and older adults, recognising their knowledge and specific needs.
educacion.closing: Media literacy is not just for students or experts. It’s a right for every person, at any stage of life, and a condition for building more democratic, informed, and empathetic societies.

tecnologia.metaDescription: Technology axis — media literacy: algorithms, privacy, digital divide, AI, and conscious use of platforms.
tecnologia.heroIntro: This axis addresses how technology shapes the way we inform ourselves, communicate, and take part in digital life. It’s not just about using devices, but about understanding how they influence what we see, think, and decide.
tecnologia.openBold: Media literacy in a technological key is not only about learning to use tools, but about understanding the systems that govern them.
paras: We live in a hyper-connected society, where devices, digital platforms, and algorithms mediate not only the information we receive, but also our emotions, decisions, and ways of relating. In this scenario, the Technology axis invites us to look beyond the interface.

Here, media literacy becomes a practice of autonomy. Because those who don’t understand how technology operates are exposed to invisible manipulations: algorithm logic, personal data collection, viralisation of hate, or the creation of information bubbles.

This axis does not seek to teach people to use technology “correctly,” but to inhabit it with awareness, question it with critical thinking, and transform it with ethics. It means shaping citizens who can protect their privacy, spot biases in automated systems, detect AI-generated content, and demand a fairer and more transparent digital environment.
tecnologia.closing: Technology and media intersect in everyday life. Understanding that intersection is key to digital citizenship.

comunicacion.sectionTitle: Keys to understanding the media world

tabs.label: Media ecosystem
paragraphs: It is the set of media, platforms, and actors that produce and spread information. It ranges from major channels to social networks and community media. Understanding who communicates, how, and with what interests is key to reading what we see more clearly.

tabs.label: Freedom of Expression and the Right to Information
paragraphs: Freedom of expression is the right to say what we think, to share ideas, opinions, and beliefs without fear of censorship or punishment. But it also includes the right to receive truthful, diverse, and timely information—something essential for making informed decisions in everyday life.

This right is not absolute: it does not protect speech that incites hatred, violence, or discrimination. That is why exercising freedom of expression also means responsibility: thinking about the consequences of what we share and fostering respectful dialogue, even when we disagree.

The right to information guarantees that all people can access reliable, transparent, and diverse content. That includes quality public media, open data, and mechanisms that let us know how decisions that affect us are made. When these rights are upheld, civic participation, social trust, and shared life are strengthened.

tabs.label: Media
paragraphs: Media help shape the image we have of the world. But they do not always show its full diversity. Sometimes certain voices, territories, or experiences are less represented. That is why it is important to broaden our view: including different perspectives helps us understand reality better and strengthen more open, plural, and respectful communication.

tabs.label: Disinformation (information integrity)
paragraphs: Disinformation (information integrity) exists because some people want to manipulate what we think, create confusion, or gain economic, political, or social advantage. Sometimes it is created on purpose; other times it spreads through error or lack of knowledge. Social networks and digital media allow this content to spread very quickly, without filters or verification.
Fighting it is not censorship: it is defending the right to be well informed, to think autonomously, and to participate responsibly in the world we share.

tabs.label: Social networks
paragraphs: On social networks, we often see only ideas similar to our own. This happens because algorithms show us what we already like or already believe. Information bubbles form this way, reinforcing our views and isolating us from other opinions. To break out of that bubble, it is essential to seek different sources, compare information, and stay open to dialogue.

educacion.sectionTitle: Keys to learning with critical awareness

tabs.label: Critical Thinking
paragraphs: It is not just about having opinions, but knowing why we hold them. Critical thinking is the ability to observe, interpret, and question the world around us—including the media messages we consume. In an environment saturated with stimuli, learning to pause, analyse, and form our own judgments becomes a key competence for autonomy and citizenship.

tabs.label: Media Literacy in the Classroom
paragraphs: Media literacy is not just another subject; it is a way of seeing and teaching the world. Integrating it in the classroom means teaching students to live with information, build knowledge collaboratively, and engage with the digital environment meaningfully. From childhood through adulthood, media literacy enables pedagogy that is more connected to reality and more aware of its impacts.

tabs.label: Content Production
paragraphs: Today we are all potential broadcasters. Creating content is not just a technical skill; it is a way of intervening in the world. Learning to produce messages (videos, podcasts, memes, texts) with purpose, ethics, and a critical eye makes it possible to exercise citizenship online and to dialogue from the local to the global. It also teaches us to listen and build with others.

tabs.label: Evaluating Information
paragraphs: The ability to distinguish reliable information from doubtful content is one of the fundamental literacies of the 21st century. Consuming data is not enough: we must learn to verify, identify sources, and recognise bias. Evaluating information does not mean distrusting everything, but learning to look closely and value well-founded knowledge.

tabs.label: Digital Life and Coexistence
paragraphs: Being online is not just a technical experience; it is a human one. Media literacy promotes forms of digital coexistence that respect diversity, encourage dialogue, and reject violence. Learning to live online means knowing how to protect ourselves, but also how to build more empathetic, collaborative, and democratic environments.

cultura.sectionTitle: The keys to understanding culture in media literacy begin with recognising that every form of expression reflects identities, contexts, and values

tabs.label: Culture is diverse
paragraphs: Culture is not single, homogeneous, or static. It is multiple, changing, and alive. Media literacy invites us to recognise that diversity as a value, not an obstacle. Understanding that there are different ways of seeing, narrating, and inhabiting the world—from a rural community to a digital urban collective—is essential for building inclusive citizenship based on mutual respect and intercultural dialogue. It is not just about accepting difference, but learning from it.

tabs.label: Media represent (and omit)
paragraphs: Every media content is a construction. No medium shows reality as it is; it selects, ranks, and frames. That is why it is essential to ask: what is shown? what is hidden? who tells the story? Media literacy seeks to build a critical gaze on those representations, understanding that what appears on screen also shapes stereotypes, power relations, and inequalities. Recognising what is omitted is the first step toward more just narratives.

tabs.label: The digital is also culture
paragraphs: TikToks, memes, emojis, X threads, reels, podcasts… all of that is language, identity, and expression. They are new ways of narrating the everyday, the political, and the intimate. Media literacy cannot treat these productions as superficial; they are part of contemporary culture. Understanding their codes, aesthetics, and modes of circulation is fundamental for dialogue with new generations and for validating the ways they make sense of the world.

tabs.label: Creating is participating
paragraphs: In digital culture, we are no longer only receivers—we are also broadcasters. Making a video, sharing a meme, writing a comment… these are communicative acts. And all communication is political, because it expresses visions, feelings, and positions. Media literacy encourages people to exercise their right to tell their story from their place, with their voice and their media. Participating actively is exercising cultural citizenship; it is inscribing oneself in the present with dignity and meaning.

tabs.label: Dialogue creates meaning
paragraphs: Neither media nor algorithms replace human encounter. Understanding does not arise from monologue, but from exchange. Dialogue—between generations, territories, and knowledges—is the heart of democratic culture. Media literacy proposes creating real spaces for conversation, where we listen carefully, disagree respectfully, and build collective knowledge. Because understanding others is also understanding ourselves in a shared world.

tabs.label: Communicating is a right
paragraphs: Having access to the internet is not enough: we need a voice. Being able to speak, be heard, and express ourselves without fear is an essential part of full citizenship. Media literacy, from a human-rights perspective, does not only seek to protect against risk (such as fake news or hate speech), but to enable the expressive potential of all people. Communicating is not a luxury; it is a condition for participating in public life freely and meaningfully.

tecnologia.sectionTitle: Keys to understanding technology in media literacy

tabs.label: Algorithms and Information Bias
paragraphs: Technology is not neutral. What we see on social networks, search engines, or platforms is mediated by algorithms that prioritise certain content and silence others. Understanding how these systems work is key to developing a critical view of the information we consume. It is not just about knowing they exist, but understanding their impact on our decisions, perceptions, and relationships.

tabs.label: Privacy and Digital Footprint
paragraphs: Every click leaves a mark. In the digital world, our data is currency. Knowing how to protect privacy is not just a technical matter, but an act of autonomy. Understanding what we share, with whom, and for what purpose helps us exercise more conscious control over our digital identity and our rights.

tabs.label: Digital Divide and Access
paragraphs: Technology amplifies inequalities when access is not guaranteed for everyone. This axis also makes visible the barriers that prevent full participation in the digital environment—from lack of connectivity to absence of training. Educating in technology with a critical approach is also educating for social justice.

tabs.label: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Culture
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence is no longer science fiction. From virtual assistants to systems that generate content, AI is part of today's information environment. Educating in this context means not only using these technologies, but also understanding how they work and developing a critical view of their impact on how we communicate, learn, and live together.

tabs.label: Conscious Use of Platforms
paragraphs: Being constantly connected does not always mean being healthily connected. This axis invites reflection on our digital habits: the time we spend, the emotions they generate, the bonds we build. It promotes balance between online and offline life, and teaches us to use technology with purpose, intention, and care.

somos.heroTitle: We strengthen capacities to understand, assess, and use information with more judgment and meaning
intro: At Precisar we work with organisations that want to strengthen people’s relationship with information and promote a more conscious, useful, and constructive use of technology.

We work with municipalities, educational communities, civil society organisations, public services, media outlets, and territorial networks to translate a complex problem — the unequal capacity to understand, assess, and use information — into concrete tools, methodologies, and resources adapted to real contexts.
somos.principle: We don’t work from closed solutions. We start from context, listen to how people experience this problem, and design with each partner ways to address it with practical sense, clear language, and capacity to implement.

problem.title: What problem we address
paras: We understand information in a broad sense. It refers not only to news or journalistic content, but also to institutional, civic, digital or non-digital, educational, and practical information that people receive, interpret, and use to solve problems, take part in public matters, access rights, and operate in digital environments.

Today the issue is no longer only connectivity. Although connectivity has advanced, a deep gap remains in people’s actual capacity to understand, assess, and use information usefully in everyday and civic life.

That gap is not limited to news or social media. It also includes institutional, educational, practical, and service-related information: the kind people need to orient themselves, solve problems, interact with institutions, and make informed decisions.

When that capacity is missing, confusion grows, distinguishing reliable information becomes harder, communication between institutions and citizens weakens, and barriers to participating, understanding, and acting with judgment widen.

items.title: We co-design with context
items.body: We don’t apply one-size-fits-all formulas. We adapt methodologies, tools, and resources to the needs, languages, and capacities of each organisation and the communities they work with.

items.title: We translate evidence into action
items.body: We produce and organise useful evidence to understand how people get informed, what barriers they face, and which tools can be more effective in supporting them.

items.title: We test in the field
items.body: We design and implement experiences in real contexts, with concrete audiences and diverse conditions, to learn, adjust, and leave replicable models.

items.title: We transfer capacities
items.body: We aim for organisations to take ownership of methodologies, resources, and tools, integrating them into their own practices beyond a one-off intervention.

items.title: We combine clarity, technology, and public purpose
items.body: We develop open tools, accessible content, and applied experiences that help people better understand how information circulates and how to use technology in a more conscious and productive way.

items.title: Diagnosis and listening
items.body: Processes to understand how different audiences get informed, what difficulties they face, and what kind of support they need.

items.title: Methodologies for territories and institutions
items.body: Design and implementation of working models for municipalities, schools, organisations, and public services.

items.title: Open resources and tools
items.body: Guides, activities, explanatory materials, participatory experiences, and conversational tools adapted to different audiences and life stages.

items.title: Support for institutional adoption
items.body: Support to teams and organisations to incorporate this agenda from their own roles, capacities, and objectives.

items.title: Evidence for decisions
items.body: Systematising lessons learned and generating useful inputs to improve practices, programmes, and ways of communicating.

outcomes.title: What we aim to leave behind
outcomes.prologue: Our goal is not simply to run activities. We aim for every organisation we work with to be left with:
items: Better tools to understand how their audiences relate to information
Usable resources adaptable to their reality
Methodologies tested in real contexts
Capacities to sustain this work over time
A stronger connection between evidence, communication, and action

approach.title: Our approach to collaboration
paras: We believe that tools work better when they are born from real use, local context, and people’s experience.

That’s why at Precisar we understand collaboration as a process of joint construction. We bring evidence, methodological design, pedagogical experience, and tool development; our partners bring territorial knowledge, community reach, local legitimacy, and implementation capacity. That combination allows us to build responses that are more relevant, clearer, and more sustainable.

why.title: Why work with Precisar
why.prologue: Because we combine four capacities that don’t usually come together:
items: Useful evidence to understand how people get informed and what they need.
Applied methodologies to translate that evidence into concrete intervention.
Accessible resources designed for different audiences and contexts.
Institutional support so capacities stay in place.

cta.title: Let’s talk
cta.body: If your organisation wants to develop tools, methodologies, or experiences to strengthen people’s relationship with information and promote a more conscious, useful, and constructive use of technology, we’d be glad to talk.

team.title: Team
team.phrase: Precisar is made by those who teach, those who create, those who think about technology, those who make decisions, neighbors, and people who, at some point, chose not to stay with the doubt. They are in every conversation we hold, in every question they ask us, in every story they allow us to tell. Without knowing it, each of them already is Precisar.

aprenderDigital.metaTitle: Learn Digital: It's Never Too Late · Precisar
aprenderDigital.metaDescription: A safe, friendly space where adults and older people build confidence and digital skills.
aprenderDigital.heroSub: A safe, welcoming, friendly space where adults and older people build confidence, gain useful digital and media skills, and enjoy connecting with their surroundings, community, and loved ones.
aprenderDigital.objectivesIntro: We train participants for a full and safe digital life.

modulos.desc: We teach how to identify disinformation (information integrity), recognise bias, and develop critical thinking to navigate the digital world in an informed way. This will help you judge whether information is truthful and protect yourself from misleading content.

You will learn to identify and avoid online fraud, protect your personal data, and manage your privacy on networks and apps, ensuring a calm, risk-free digital experience. We will give you the tools to feel safe with every click.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the ability of machines to imitate and perform tasks that require human intelligence. We will explore how AI is transforming our daily lives and the future, discover its practical applications, and learn how to interact with it consciously.

Find a healthy balance between time spent online and in-person activities, using digital tools to enrich your life and strengthen social bonds without replacing face-to-face interaction. We promote conscious, beneficial use of technology.

contextParas: Although 96.5% of Chile's population has some form of connectivity, that coverage does not automatically translate into safe, autonomous navigation skills in the digital environment.

We live in a historic moment marked by technological advances that expand the possibilities of producing and sharing information, but also create an ecosystem saturated with haste, immediacy, and difficulty building deep relationships.
The benefits and, above all, the risks of our interaction with media and technologies have placed media and digital education as a tool that should be integrated into the agenda of many institutions.

Recognising access to these tools as a right is not enough: they must be incorporated into formal education and debate spaces opened beyond classrooms, especially for those no longer in the school system.

Having the opportunity to understand digital culture and participate critically is key for adults and older people. That gap amplifies their vulnerabilities, limiting access to the labour market, reliable information, basic services, and other fundamental rights.
It is imperative to design and implement solid policies, allocate adequate resources, and foster partnerships with companies and organisations across sectors.
Only then can we democratise access to media and digital education, ensuring people of all ages develop autonomy and critical thinking, both online and offline.

items.label: Media education
items.body: In this core module we will equip you with tools to navigate the vast information ecosystem. You will learn to identify disinformation (information integrity) and fake news, recognise implicit bias in various content including AI-generated material, and distinguish manipulated images and videos. You will develop critical thinking that helps you judge whether information is truthful, protect yourself from misleading narratives, and consume media consciously and in an informed way.

items.label: Artificial Intelligence

items.label: Digital wellbeing

docentes.metaTitle: Digital Media Education for Teachers · Precisar
docentes.metaDescription: Teaching resources, classroom guides, and workshops to help teachers prepare students for a conscious, safe, and participatory digital present.
docentes.heroSub: Prepare your students for a conscious, safe, and participatory digital present. We provide teaching resources, classroom guides, and practical activities that strengthen critical evaluation of information, responsible content creation, and coexistence in digital environments. A tool for your classes that means not more work, but more confidence, safety, and reflection for you and your students in the digital world.

objetivos.desc: Train teachers to help students critically evaluate information, identify disinformation (information integrity), and recognise bias in various digital sources, including AI-generated content.
Provide educators with tools to guide students in creating digital content ethically and responsibly, respecting copyright and promoting constructive messages.
Train teachers to instruct their students on active, safe, and respectful participation on digital networks and platforms, fostering digital citizenship.
Facilitate integration of digital media education into the school curriculum, providing guides and resources adapted to different subjects and educational levels.

docentes.benefitsIntro: Strengthen teacher training and transform your students' educational experience.

beneficios.desc: Help your students develop skills to think critically, recognise false content, and act with confidence and respect in the digital world.

Strengthen your teaching team with practical tools, an updated pedagogical approach, and confidence to face digital environment challenges. Train them to guide students in critical, safe, and creative use of technology and to lead educational innovation in their school communities.
Create a learning environment where students, teachers, and families collaborate for more conscious and ethical use of technology.
By incorporating good data protection and privacy practices, risks of cyberbullying and misuse of technology are significantly reduced, ensuring a safer digital environment.

metodologia.desc: 4 live Zoom sessions with hands-on activities and self-paced work on the EducaMedios Programme digital platform, so each teacher can progress at their own pace.

docentes.modulesIntro: Step by step, module by module.

modulos.label: Foundations of Digital Media Education
modulos.desc: Understand, teach, and transform. Explore the impact of media and digital platforms on everyday life and their link to educational goals. Learn to integrate media and digital education in the classroom through applied projects such as content creation, critical analysis of information, and guided debate, strengthening the teacher's role as a trainer of active digital citizenship.

modulos.label: Disinformation (information integrity), Data Verification
modulos.desc: Acquire practical strategies to teach your students to identify and dismantle disinformation (information integrity): they will learn data verification techniques, use of fact-checking tools, and methods to compare sources, recognise manipulation patterns, and apply these skills in school research and daily life.

modulos.label: Algorithms and Artificial Intelligence
modulos.desc: Deepen your understanding of how algorithms and Artificial Intelligence influence what we see online, from social networks to search engines. We will analyse inherent AI bias and its impact on information, and give you tools to teach students to critically evaluate content generated or filtered by these technologies. You will also learn to establish clear conditions of use —such as digital responsibility agreements, criteria for selecting automated sources, and teacher-student collaborative projects— that foster a safe, reflective environment for exploring AI in the classroom.

modulos.label: Digital Content Production and Citizenship
modulos.desc: This module will train you to guide your students in creating responsible, meaningful digital content. We will explore tools for producing text, image, and video, focusing on ethics, respect for intellectual property, and the impact of their messages. We will foster active, constructive participation in the digital space, turning students into conscious, responsible creators.

modulos.label: Security, Privacy, and Digital Wellbeing
modulos.desc: Learn to address crucial topics such as cybersecurity, personal data protection, and privacy management with your students. You will develop strategies to promote healthy, balanced use of technology, prevent cyberbullying, and foster digital wellbeing that integrates online and offline life.

modulos.label: Curricular Integration and Media Education Projects
modulos.desc: Discover how to integrate digital media education across subjects and educational levels. We will provide examples of successful projects and guide you in designing practical activities that let your students apply their knowledge, culminating in meaningful projects that demonstrate their digital and media education.

pensamientoCritico.metaDescription: Two workshops: news verification and media literacy in the AI era. Online and in-person formats for teams and communities.
pensamientoCritico.heroSub: Tools to identify, analyse, and verify information circulating in the digital world.
introParas: To meet this challenge, courses have been designed to turn participants into critical, competent consumers, giving them the tools needed to identify, analyse, and verify the information they find in today's digital ecosystem.
We understand that each person has different needs, which is why we offer two ways to take the courses.

modalidades.title: Online format
modalidades.text: A facilitator once a week. Each 90-minute session with practical activities with participants.

modalidades.title: In-person format
modalidades.text: Experiential workshops in small groups, maximum 15 people, with practical exercises, group dynamics, and printed materials.

pensamientoCritico.taller1Kicker: Don't let them fool you! Learn to verify what you read online.
taller1Body: Do you receive WhatsApp chains or see news on Facebook and wonder if they are true? This workshop is a guide of tools and practical tips to help you tell real information from false in minutes. The goal is for you to feel safer browsing the internet and confident about what to believe and what to dismiss.

Aimed at anyone who uses social networks and wants to learn to protect themselves from deception and disinformation (information integrity). You don't need to know anything about technology — just be curious.
pensamientoCritico.outcomesLead: By the end you will be able to:
taller1Outcomes: Apply a 3-step checklist to evaluate any news item.
Recognise the most common warning signs in fake news.
Use free tools to tell whether a photo is real or outdated.
Talk calmly with friends or family who share false information.

taller1Modulos.title: Why is fake news so appealing?
taller1Modulos.desc: Shocking or anger-provoking headlines are designed to make us share without thinking. Understanding this is the first step to avoid the trap.

taller1Modulos.title: The 3-step method: Pause, Question, and Compare
taller1Modulos.desc: Pause: Don't share immediately. Question: Who says this? Why? Compare: Does any reputable outlet report the same thing?

taller1Modulos.title: Easy tools at your fingertips
taller1Modulos.desc: A practical workshop where you will learn to use Google's reverse image search on your own phone.

taller1Modulos.title: What do I do now?
taller1Modulos.desc: A personal action plan for consuming information more healthily and tips for acting when someone shares something false.

pensamientoCritico.taller2Title: Media and Digital Literacy in the AI Era
pensamientoCritico.taller2Kicker: Understanding the Digital World: How AI and Algorithms decide what you see.
taller2Body: Do you feel Instagram reads your mind or YouTube always knows what video to recommend? It's not magic — it's algorithms and artificial intelligence. In this workshop we open the hood of the internet so you can simply understand how these technologies organise the content you consume every day and how this affects your view of the world.
Aimed at anyone curious about how social networks work behind the scenes and the impact technology has on our lives.
taller2Outcomes: Explain what an algorithm is using a simple example.
Understand how platforms personalise the content they show you.
Recognise the filter bubble effect in your daily life.
Identify new ways AI is used to create both real and fake content.

taller2Modulos.title: The secret chef of your internet: What is an algorithm?
taller2Modulos.desc: Everyday examples like a cooking recipe to explain what an algorithm is and how Spotify, Netflix, Facebook, and Instagram use them.

taller2Modulos.title: A world made for you: Personalisation and the bubble
taller2Modulos.desc: How platforms learn from your preferences to build a profile about you and the filter bubble phenomenon.

taller2Modulos.title: The arrival of Artificial Intelligence
taller2Modulos.desc: What AI is, how it can generate images, texts, and voices that seem real, how it is used positively, and what its risks are.

taller2Modulos.title: How to navigate a world with AI?
taller2Modulos.desc: Practical tips for moving in this new landscape and valuing reliable information sources.

sections.title:
Digital culture
that travels
sections.body: At the Conscious Digital Hub we immerse ourselves in digital culture through interactive, thematic exhibits. Each one is portable and designed to explore how media and technology influence our society, bringing knowledge directly to events, municipalities, public spaces, and more.

groups.label: Where and for whom?
items: Squares, libraries, cultural venues, schools, auditoriums, and corporate events.
Designed for a broad audience of any age and educational level.
Each visitor gains critical perspectives on digital culture and practical tools.

groups.label: Our approach
items: We don't just present topics: we also open a space for dialogue and action.
We translate complex concepts — disinformation (information integrity), AI, privacy — into accessible sensory experiences.
We foster meaningful conversations about responsible technology use.

sections.title:
What you'll
find
sections.body: We offer a combination of visual and hands-on elements that will captivate your participants from the first moment.

groups.label: Elements of each exhibit
items: Visually striking posters — Designed to spark immediate conversation and reflection on crucial topics in contemporary technology. Each poster acts as an 'eye-opener' presenting information clearly and aesthetically.
Interactive applications — Invite first-hand experimentation with cutting-edge technologies such as augmented reality and AI to create memorable experiences that connect with audiences playfully.
Video animations — Lead to deep discussions about privacy and detecting fake news. Explore ethical dilemmas of the digital world through visual stories.
Hands-on experiences — Stimulate meaningful debate among participants. The perfect complement before workshops, talks, or seminars on digital culture.

Installation
models

Recommended duration: 2 weeks – permanent
Audience: 200–500 people per day

sections.title:
10 ways to
implement
sections.body: They can be integrated in multiple ways into your event's space and timeline, without being limited to a specific audience.

groups.label: Implementation possibilities
items: 01 · Pre-event activation — Deploy interactive modules in corridors or lobbies so the audience discovers key concepts before any scheduled activity.
02 · Thematic meeting points — Create stations dedicated to privacy, AI, disinformation (information integrity), or digital ethics, allowing visitors to move freely between them.
03 · Self-guided routes — Design a chronological or logical path guiding people through different challenges and experiences, each supported by visual and multimedia materials.
04 · Mobile elements — Use tablets, portable kiosks, or augmented reality glasses to bring the installation to small or itinerant spaces within the same venue.
05 · Downloadable material — Offer visitors QR codes linking to guides, infographics, and digital resources to explore after the event.
06 · Reflection rooms — Enable areas with comfortable furniture where short discussion videos or expert panels are projected, inviting spontaneous dialogue.
07 · Live AI interaction — Include chatbots or virtual assistants that answer questions, generate privacy profile analyses, and offer personalised recommendations.
08 · Immersive experiences — Incorporate 360° video projections, virtual reality, and sound environments to immerse visitors in scenarios illustrating technological risks and opportunities.
09 · Gamification — Implement challenges and games based on questions about chosen topics, rewarding participation with digital badges or physical recognition.
10 · Integration with talks — Combine interactive stations with conferences so each speaker can refer to specific modules to illustrate their arguments.

programsFuncionarios.heroTitle:
Media Literacy Training
for Public Officials.
programsFuncionarios.heroSub: Training designed specifically for the context of public administration.
programsFuncionarios.porQue1: In today's digital environment, disinformation (information integrity) and information manipulation are not only a social challenge, but a direct risk to public administration, citizen trust, and democratic stability.
programsFuncionarios.porQue2: Public servants' ability to navigate, evaluate, and use media effectively and safely is a fundamental competence.
programsFuncionarios.porQue3: This programme has been designed specifically for the context of public administration. Its goal is to equip officials with the tools they need to work safely, reliably, and efficiently in a media-saturated world, strengthening institutional transparency, citizen participation, and resilience to information threats.
programsFuncionarios.estructuraSub: 8 sessions designed for the context of public administration.

cursoTabs.label: Session 1
cursoTabs.panelTitle: Session 1: A Life Full of Media
cursoTabs.body: Introduces the central role of media in society and the four levels of media analysis: platform, content, industry, and environment. A structured view of how media build realities and shape decisions in public and civic life.

cursoTabs.label: Session 2
cursoTabs.panelTitle: Session 2: How Do Digital Media Work?
cursoTabs.body: Explores the impact of digitalisation and how algorithms, echo chambers, and polarisation work. Understand why people receive different information on their devices and how this affects citizens' perception of public management.

cursoTabs.label: Sess. 3 & 4
cursoTabs.panelTitle: Sessions 3 and 4: Reliability and Evaluation of Information
cursoTabs.body: Focuses on managing information overload and evaluating source reliability, considering author, context, and content. Covers deepfakes and intentional disinformation (information integrity). Practical tools for verifying before communicating or making institutional decisions.

cursoTabs.label: Session 5
cursoTabs.body: Provides tools for interaction and effective communication, and for fostering citizen participation through media. How to respond, clarify, and communicate from public institutions with transparency and judgment.

cursoTabs.label: Session 6
cursoTabs.panelTitle: Session 6: Use of Social Networks in Public Administration
cursoTabs.body: Addresses the opportunities and responsibilities of social network use, emphasising that officials must act impartially, independently, and fairly. Protocols, good practices, and ethical limits for institutional and personal use of digital platforms.

cursoTabs.label: Sess. 7 & 8
cursoTabs.body: Allows participants to reflect on the goals of media literacy in their work and assess their learning for practical application. Closes with a personal action plan and concrete commitments to apply in the institution.

beneficios.title: Informed Decision-making
beneficios.desc: Officials will be trained to search for, filter, and evaluate relevant and reliable information, improving the quality of internal decisions and daily performance.

beneficios.title: Improved Public Communication
beneficios.desc: Tools for more effective and transparent communication through media and social networks, increasing citizens' trust in the institution.

beneficios.title: Reduced Institutional Risks
beneficios.desc: By understanding algorithms and echo chambers and learning to identify disinformation (information integrity), deepfakes, and propaganda, officials protect institutional reputation.

beneficios.title: Fostering a Culture of Critical Thinking
beneficios.desc: An analytical mindset is promoted among staff, enabling them to approach information reflectively and consciously — essential for modern public management.

blocks.text: This Privacy Policy and Personal Data Processing Policy (hereinafter, the "Privacy Policy") aims to inform participants in the citizen consultation "How do you get informed today?" (hereinafter, the "Consultation"), promoted by Fundación Democracia Abierta and its Precisar initiative (hereinafter, "DemocraTICa" or "we"), about how we collect, use, store, share and protect your personal data, in accordance with current Chilean legislation and international best practices in the field.

DemocraTICa is committed to respecting and protecting your privacy and personal data. This policy has been drafted in compliance with current Chilean regulations, Law No. 19,628 on Protection of Private Life (in its current version) and the new Law No. 21,719 on Personal Data Protection, which modernizes the legislation and aligns it with the highest international standards, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
The controller of your personal data is:

items.text: Ana Magdalena Marín Ladrón de Guevara

sections.title: 3. What personal data do we collect?

blocks.text: Within the framework of the Consultation, we will collect the following categories of personal data:
3.1 Identification and Contact Data
Optionally, we may request data such as: email address; full name.

blocks.label: Purpose:
blocks.text: Future communications about the study results or to invite you to participate in later stages of the project.

blocks.label: Important clarification:
blocks.text: Your participation in the consultation is not conditional on providing this information. You may participate anonymously.
3.2 Sociodemographic Data

We will collect data such as: age (in ranges: 18-25, 26-35, 36-50, 51-65, 65+); gender (male, female, other, prefer not to specify); education level (primary, secondary, technical, university, postgraduate); municipality of residence; region of residence; studies (in general categories).

blocks.label: Protection:
blocks.text: This data will be requested in ranges or in anonymized form to protect your identity. Information that would allow us to identify you directly will not be collected.
3.3 Data on Information Habits and Preferences

The Consultation focuses on questions about: how you get informed; which media you use (television, radio, print press, social networks, digital platforms, etc.); how often you get informed; which formats you prefer (text, video, audio, infographics, etc.); which topics interest you (politics, economy, technology, health, etc.).
3.4 Data on Media Literacy Skills and Needs

We will collect information about: your ability to verify information; your capacity to use technology; your understanding of news and data; your ability to identify disinformation (information integrity).
3.5 Opinions and Perceptions
We will ask for your opinion on: disinformation (information integrity) and its effects; artificial intelligence in the media; possible solutions to these phenomena; trust in different media outlets.
3.6 Sensitive Data
The Consultation may include questions about: your political or ideological opinions; your religious beliefs (if applicable); any other information considered sensitive under Law 21,719.

blocks.label: Special protection:
blocks.text: Processing of this sensitive data will be carried out only with your explicit consent and with the strictest security measures. We will inform you clearly and prominently when a question involves this type of data, and you may choose not to answer without this affecting your participation in the consultation.

sections.title: 4. What do we use your personal data for?

blocks.text: The personal data we collect will be used exclusively for the following purposes:
4.1 Statistical Analysis
To generate aggregated and anonymized evidence on: information habits of citizens in Chile; information needs; perceptions of disinformation (information integrity) and media literacy.

blocks.label: Clarification:
blocks.text: Analyses will always be presented in aggregated form, with no possibility of identifying individual participants.
4.2 Academic and Social Research

The results of the Consultation will be used for: report preparation; academic studies; scientific publications; contribution to knowledge about disinformation (information integrity) and media literacy.
4.3 Prototype and Solution Design

The information collected will serve as input for: co-design of new news formats; development of information platforms; creation of educational resources; development of information verification tools.
4.4 Public Policy Advocacy
The project's findings will be shared with: decision-makers; media outlets; civil society organizations; public agencies.

blocks.label: Objective:
blocks.text: To promote public policies and practices that strengthen Chile's information ecosystem.
4.5 Communication and Outreach
If you have consented, we may use your email address to: send you information about project progress; share results and findings; invite you to participate in related future initiatives.

blocks.label: Right to withdraw consent:
blocks.text: You may withdraw this consent at any time by contacting us.
4.6 Compliance with Legal Obligations
We may use your data to: comply with legal obligations; respond to requests from competent authorities; protect our legal rights.

sections.title: 5. Legal Bases for Processing Your Data

blocks.text: 5.1 Free, Informed, Specific and Unambiguous Consent

Your participation in the Consultation is voluntary. When you start the survey, we will ask for your consent clearly and explicitly for the processing of your personal data, in accordance with the purposes described in this policy.
Characteristics of consent: free; informed; specific; unambiguous. For sensitive data: we will request additional explicit consent before collecting any data considered sensitive.
5.2 Legitimate Interest

We may process your data in anonymized and aggregated form for research and statistical purposes, within the project's legitimate interest of: generating knowledge for the public good; strengthening Chile's information ecosystem; contributing to informed public debate; improving media literacy.

blocks.label: Balancing of interests:
blocks.text: This legitimate interest does not override your fundamental rights, and data is always processed in anonymized form when this legal basis is used.

sections.title: 6. With whom do we share your personal data?

blocks.text: DemocraTICa will not sell, rent or transfer your personal data to third parties for profit. Your data may only be shared in the following circumstances:
6.1 Research Team

The DemocraTICa team and its direct collaborators will have access to the data for project purposes, under strict confidentiality agreements that include: obligation to maintain secrecy; restriction of use to project purposes; prohibition of disclosure to third parties; penalties for non-compliance.
6.2 Strategic Partners
We may share aggregated and anonymized data with: civil society organizations; universities and research centers; media outlets; public agencies.

blocks.label: Condition:
blocks.text: This data will always be shared in aggregated form, with no possibility of identifying individual participants.
6.3 Publications and Dissemination
Reports and publications derived from the project will present data in aggregated, statistical, anonymized form, with no possibility of identifying individual participants.
6.4 Legal Requirements
We may share your personal data if required by: current law; a decree or resolution; a court order.

blocks.label: Protection:
blocks.text: In these cases, we will inform the data subject about the request, unless the law expressly prohibits it.
6.5 Service Providers

We may share data with service providers that help us operate (hosting, analytics, etc.), under contracts that guarantee: equivalent data protection; exclusive use for project purposes; confidentiality obligations.

sections.title: 7. How Long Do We Retain Your Data?

blocks.text: We will retain your personal data according to the schedule published on the original site: identification and contact data (3 years from last communication, secure deletion); sociodemographic data, information habits and opinions (5 years from collection, anonymization or deletion); sensitive data (3 years from collection, secure deletion); aggregated/anonymized data (indefinite for research).

Deletion procedure: data will be securely deleted using cryptographic methods; a deletion certificate will be generated; a record of deletions will be maintained. Where possible, data will be anonymized rather than deleted; anonymized data may be retained indefinitely for research.

sections.title: 8. What Are Your Rights and How Can You Exercise Them?

blocks.text: Under Law 21,719, you have the right to:

items.text: access the personal data we hold about you. Send an email to __EMAIL__ with the subject "Personal Data Access Request", attach a copy of your ID. Response time: maximum 30 business days.
correct inaccurate data. Subject: "Personal Data Rectification Request".
when there is no legal basis, deadlines expire, you withdraw consent or object to processing. Subject: "Personal Data Erasure Request".
object to specific processing. Subject: "Data Processing Objection Request".
request portability in structured format. Subject: "Personal Data Portability Request".
at any time. Subject: "Consent Withdrawal". Future processing will stop; data already lawfully processed will not be affected.

blocks.text: To exercise any of these rights, send a request to __EMAIL__ with your full name, a copy of your ID, a clear description of what you are requesting and a signature (in case of physical submission). Acknowledgment of receipt within 2 business days; response within a maximum of 30 business days. You may appeal to the Personal Data Protection Agency if you are not satisfied.
APDP contact: website, email and phone will be provided when the APDP is operational. Deadline for filing a complaint: within 1 year from when you become aware of the facts that motivate it.

Fundación Democracia Abierta reserves the right to modify this Privacy Policy at any time. If you do not agree with significant changes, you may: withdraw your consent; request deletion of your data; contact us to discuss alternatives.
If you have any questions or concerns about this Privacy Policy or the processing of your personal data, you can contact us at __EMAIL__

footerNotes.text: This Policy takes effect as of December 31, 2025 and will apply to all data collected from that date.
When the Personal Data Protection Agency is operational, we will align with its guidelines and recommendations.
Any dispute related to this Policy will be resolved in accordance with the laws of the Republic of Chile and the jurisdiction of Chilean courts.

propuestaPoliticaAlfabetizacion.nudosTitle: Three critical knots to resolve in Chile on MLI

nudos.text: CONCEPTUAL CONFUSION — MLI reduced to tool use (digital literacy) instead of critical thinking about information and media.
INSTITUTIONAL FRAGMENTATION — 35+ valuable actors but without coordination or joint governance.
AGE GAPS — Each group (children and adolescents, adults, older adults) requires differentiated approaches.

scenarios2030.title: The cost of inaction
scenarios2030.sub: Chile's algorithmic society without a critical compass.
items: Democratic erosion: decisions manipulated by deepfakes and opaque micro-targeting.
Mass vulnerability: generative AI scams especially affect older adults.
Loss of informational sovereignty: dependence on foreign platforms without transparency.
Social fracture: unresolved digital divides.
Job precarity: replacement without reskilling.

scenarios2030.title: The opportunity of action
items: Strengthened democracy: citizens who identify manipulation and debate with evidence.
Social innovation: communities using AI for health, education and the environment.
Intergenerational inclusion: autonomous older adults; responsible youth.
Knowledge economy: collaborative work with AI and entrepreneurship.
Regional leadership: Chile as an Ibero-American reference.

No algorithmic transparency or right to explanation.

propuestaPoliticaAlfabetizacion.leyMarcoTitle: Proposal: MLI Framework Law for Chile
propuestaPoliticaAlfabetizacion.leyMarcoQuote: Guarantee that all people in Chile develop competencies to access, evaluate, use and create information critically, ethically and participatively, as a right for full democracy.

leyMarcoBlocks.body: Create specific MLI institutions. Permanent Intersectoral Table. Coordination with Education, Science, Culture, Social Development.
Curricular MLI integration in pedagogies. Mandatory competencies for graduation. Professional practice with an MLI component.
Updates on threats (generative AI). Active methodologies and MLI teacher network.
Kits by level. Digital platform and MLI activity bank.

items: Create MLI Intersectoral Table.
Design National Policy with citizen participation.
Secured 2025–2026 funding.
Define coordinating institution.

phases.title: PHASE 2 — PILOTING
items: MLI Cities in 16 municipalities.
Teacher training (initial and continuing).
National MLI Observatory.
Pedagogical resources.

phases.title: PHASE 3 — SCALING
items: Evaluate and adjust pilots.
Integrate MLI into SIMCE/ENDDEIE.
Consolidate governance.

recommendations.text: MLI institution with legal mandate. Intersectoral Table. Stable and multi-year budget.
Explicit MLI competencies. MLI in initial and continuing training.
Municipal network with local facilitators. Prioritize children and adolescents, lagging adults and older adults.
Kits by level + national platform. Private co-responsibility.
National MLI Observatory. Indicators in SIMCE and ENDDEIE.
Right to algorithmic explanation. Accessibility in digital services.

propuestaPoliticaAlfabetizacion.ctaTitle: Call to action for Chilean decision-makers
ctaColumns: Move from access to critical competencies — Chile already has connectivity; now digitally competent citizens.
Legislate to institutionalize — MLI as a citizen right with a specific regulatory framework.
Fund and measure to scale — Sustainable investment in what works, with rigorous evaluation.
propuestaPoliticaAlfabetizacion.ctaClosing: The moment is now. Each day without action: more vulnerability, deeper gaps, erosion of trust and democratic weakening. The cost of inaction will be irreversible; the benefit of action will be transformative. What Chile do we want for 2030?
